match.reason: The bank point 'Protection policies' covers protection laws in general across several states, while the new point is about one specific NSW body, the Aborigines Protection Board, with its 1883 founding and 1915 power to remove children without a court hearing, so it is a related but narrower and more specific idea.

draft.title: The Aborigines Protection Board
card: The NSW Government set up the Aborigines Protection Board in 1883. It was meant to protect Aboriginal people, but it mostly controlled their lives.
The Board decided where many Aboriginal people could live, often on reserves, and where and whether they could work.
From 1915, the Board could remove Aboriginal children from their families without a court hearing. Families had no chance to argue against it in court.
Many children were sent to training homes or to work for others. Families were broken up, and these removals caused lasting grief and loss of culture.
draft.remember: The Board, set up in 1883, controlled Aboriginal lives, and from 1915 it could remove children without a court hearing.

a.q: What new power did the Aborigines Protection Board gain in 1915?
opts: Removing children without a court hearing
Setting up the first missions in NSW
Ordering Aboriginal people to leave Australia
Giving Aboriginal families land of their choice
a.why: From 1915 the Board could take children without going to court, so families could not challenge it. The Board controlled where people lived and worked, but it did not set up missions or give families land of their choice.
a.clue: Think about what happened to children and who had to approve it.

b.q: In 1920, an officer of the Board takes a child from her family in a NSW town. What did the law at that time require before this?
opts: Nothing, as no court hearing was needed
A hearing before a judge
The family's written permission
A vote of the local council
b.why: After 1915 the Board could remove children without a court hearing. A judge, family permission or a council vote was not needed, which is why families could not challenge it.
b.clue: Remember what the 1915 change took away.

problems.detail: The right option 'Nothing, as no court hearing was needed' goes further than the card. The card says only that no court hearing was needed. Under the 1915 amendment the Board still had to judge removal to be in the child's moral or physical welfare. 'Nothing' could teach that no condition at all applied. Better: 'No court hearing; the Board could decide itself.'

proposal.title: The Aborigines Protection Board
card: The NSW Government set up the Aborigines Protection Board in 1883. It was meant to protect Aboriginal people, but it mostly controlled their lives.
The Board decided where many Aboriginal people could live, often on reserves, and where and whether they could work.

From 1915, the Board could remove Aboriginal children from their families if it decided this was for the child's welfare. It did not need a court hearing, so families had no chance to argue their case before a judge.
Many children were sent to training homes or to work for others. Families were broken up, and these removals caused lasting grief and loss of culture.

b.q: In 1920, an officer of the Board takes a child from her family in a NSW town. Under the law at that time, who decided the child could be removed?
opts: The Board itself, without going to court
A judge, after hearing from the family
The child's parents, by signing a form
The local council, by holding a vote
